objective: Managing increments: aligning each increment to business priorities, defining increment goals, and demonstrating value through early feedback
secondaryObjectives: Managing value delivery: defining what value looks like (success criteria, sustainability, security, compliance) and confirming targeted results were actually achieved

sources.cite: PMI, PMI Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP) Examination Content Outline (March 2026): Mindset 28%, Leadership 25%, Product 19%, Delivery 28%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of PMI's PDF. Relevant text: Domain IV Task 1 'Seek early feedback' ('Deliver work in small increments'; 'Collect and incorporate stakeholders' feedback on a regular basis'); Task 3 'Manage impediments and risk' ('Proactively identify risks and impediments'; 'Prioritize impediment removal and risk mitigation activities'); Domain I Task 7 'Embrace Change' ('Embrace process adaptation by responding to changing requirements and priorities'; 'Adapt to product needs based on the learning and feedback'). The objective wording here is the course seed's. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's sprint-release-before-review-pmiacp (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The company, the product, the team and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the agile project lead for Kestrel Boilers' field-service app, a fictional heating company. The sponsor wants everything delivered in one release in three months. Ten technicians have volunteered to pilot early versions.
handover: Backlog: 60 items across parts, signatures, scheduling, invoicing and reporting.
The biggest cost today is paperwork errors in parts used, which delay invoices.
howItWorks: The board shows the Sprint's commitments, the work, the impediments, the people's support and the Scrum events.
Move on a day at a time. A decision comes to you at each Daily Scrum; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Day 2: the scheduling screen demos well, but invoice delays are unchanged and the CFO questions the project.
Day 3 (at release): technicians find the parts screen unusable with gloves on in cold basements; the whole release needs rework.
Day 4: technicians go back to paper; adoption in the pilot drops to two of ten.

goalPrompt.title: What should this increment deliver?
goalPrompt.context: The sponsor wants scheduling first because it's the most visible feature.

choices.label: Set the increment goal on parts recording and signatures, the cause of 62% of invoice delays, with a measurable success criterion

effects.log: The increment targets parts and signatures.

choices.feedback: Increments are ordered by business value and given a goal that makes value testable.

choices.label: Take a little of everything
choices.feedback: Nothing useful is finished; feedback is shallow.

choices.label: Build scheduling first because the sponsor finds it most visible
choices.feedback: The visible feature isn't the valuable one; invoice delays continue.

feedbackPrompt.title: When do technicians see it?
feedbackPrompt.context: Parts recording works on test phones; signatures are half done.

choices.label: Put the working parts recording in the ten pilot technicians' hands this week and watch them use it on real jobs

effects.log: Pilot technicians use it on jobs.

choices.feedback: Early feedback from real use reveals what demos miss.

choices.label: Demo it to technicians in the office
choices.feedback: Useful, but an office demo misses conditions on site.

choices.label: Wait until everything is finished
choices.feedback: Feedback after three months means three months of guesses.

adaptPrompt.title: Technicians say gloves don't work on the small buttons
adaptPrompt.context: They also want a barcode scan for parts.

choices.label: Re-order the backlog: larger touch targets now, barcode scan next; measure invoice errors from pilot jobs against the baseline

effects.log: The backlog adapts; errors fall from 12% to 3% on pilot jobs.

choices.feedback: Feedback changes the plan, and the success criterion confirms the value.

choices.label: Log the feedback for later
choices.feedback: The feedback is kept but doesn't change the plan.

choices.label: Dismiss it: the design was approved
choices.feedback: Ignoring users' feedback wastes the reason for early increments.

reflection.question: Write the increment notes for the sponsor: why this increment, what the pilot showed, and the value measured.

parts.label: Goal and feedback
parts.criteria: Parts and signatures first by value; pilot on real jobs.

parts.label: Value
parts.criteria: Backlog adapted; invoice errors from 12% to 3% on pilot jobs.
parts.modelAnswer: We enlarged touch targets and queued barcode scanning; invoice errors on pilot jobs fell from 12% to 3%.

scoring.modelReasoning: Each increment is aligned to business priorities with a goal that makes its value testable. Early feedback from real users on a usable slice reveals what demos miss, and the backlog adapts to it. Value delivery is confirmed by measuring the targeted results against a baseline, not by shipping features.
